lessons.title: Spray drying: principles and equipment
lessons.body: Spray drying turns a liquid detergent slurry into dry powder in one step. You pump the slurryâabout 60-70% waterâinto a tall drying chamber through a nozzle or spinning disc. Hot air (200-300Â°C) meets the droplets, water evaporates in seconds, and dry particles fall to the bottom. In Africa, small plants often use a box-type spray dryer made locally from mild steel, with a kerosene or gas burner. A 100 kg/hour unit costs around $15,000â$25,000. Key parts: feed pump, atomizer, air heater, cyclone, and bag filter. The atomizer is criticalâa worn nozzle gives big, wet lumps. Check nozzle pressure daily; it should be 20â30 bar for pressure nozzles. For a spinning disc, speed is 10,000â20,000 rpm. Inlet air temperature should be 250â300Â°C; outlet 90â100Â°C. If outlet drops below 80Â°C, powder will be sticky. In humid African climates, preheat the air to avoid condensation. Start by mixing your slurry: 30% active detergent, 40% sodium sulphate, 10% sodium silicate, 5% sodium carbonate, and water to balance. Keep slurry at 60â70Â°C and stir continuously. A simple test: dip a glass rod, let it coolâif it forms a hard film, solids are right. Never let slurry sit overnight; it separates. After drying, powder goes to a cyclone where fine dust is separated, then to a bag filter. Collect powder from both. Yield should be 95% of solids. Energy use: about 1.2 kg of fuel oil per kg of water evaporated. In Nigeria or Kenya, use rice husk or sawdust burners to cut costs. Always wear a dust mask and gogglesâfine detergent dust irritates eyes and lungs. Clean the chamber daily to prevent caking.

lessons.title: Agglomeration and granulation techniques
lessons.body: Agglomeration makes powder particles stick together into larger, free-flowing granules. This reduces dust and makes the product dissolve faster. The simplest method is batch granulation in a concrete mixer or rotating drum. You start with dry base powder (spray-dried or mixed), then spray a liquid binderâusually a 40% sodium silicate solution or waterâwhile tumbling. For 100 kg of powder, use 10â15 liters of binder. Mix for 5â10 minutes until you see small balls forming. Stop before they become too big. A good granule is 0.5â2 mm. Test by squeezing a handful: it should hold shape but crumble easily. If it sticks to your hand, too much binder. For small-scale production, a pan granulator (like a tilted rotating disc) works well. Set the disc angle at 45â50 degrees and speed at 20â30 rpm. Feed powder continuously and spray binder at the top. The granules roll and grow. Discharge at the bottom. In Africa, you can build a pan granulator from a 200-liter drum cut in half, mounted on a shaft with a small motor. Cost: under $500. Another method is extrusion: push wet paste through a screen with 1â2 mm holes, then dry the strands. This gives uniform granules. For detergent bars, you can use a meat mincer as a small extruder. After granulation, dry the granules in a tray dryer at 60â70Â°C for 2â3 hours until moisture is below 5%. Then sieve to remove fines and oversize. Fines go back to the mixer; oversize is crushed. Always add 1â2% of a anti-caking agent like sodium aluminosilicate before packing. Store granules in lined bags to keep out humidity. In coastal areas, use silica gel sachets in storage bins.

lessons.title: Fluid bed processing
lessons.body: A fluid bed processor blows hot air upward through a bed of powder, making it behave like a boiling liquid. This is used for drying, granulating, and coating detergent powders. For small African workshops, a fluid bed dryer can be made from a 200-liter drum with a perforated bottom plate (2 mm holes), a fan, and a heater. Air velocity must be high enough to lift particles but not blow them out. For 1â2 mm granules, use 1.5â2.5 m/s air speed. Inlet air temperature: 80â120Â°C. You can dry 50 kg of granules in 20â30 minutes, much faster than tray drying. To granulate in a fluid bed, start with dry powder, fluidize it, then spray binder (water or silicate solution) from a nozzle at the top. The particles stick together and grow. Stop when you reach the desired size. This is called top-spray granulation. For coating, spray a solution of polymer or wax to protect the detergent from moisture. A common coating is 2% polyethylene glycol (PEG) 4000. In Africa, fluid bed dryers are used in tea and coffee processing, so you can learn from those factories. Key controls: air flow, inlet temperature, and spray rate. If the bed temperature drops below 40Â°C, particles become sticky and defluidize. If it rises above 80Â°C, binder dries too fast and you get dust. Always start with a low spray rate, then increase. After processing, cool the powder with unheated air for 5 minutes before discharging. Clean the filter bags every batchâdetergent dust clogs them quickly. Safety: fine detergent dust can explode if ignited. Ground all equipment and use explosion-proof motors. Never open the chamber while hot air is flowing.

lessons.title: Particle size distribution and control
lessons.body: Particle size distribution (PSD) means the range of particle sizes in your powder. For detergents, you want most particles between 0.2 mm and 2 mm. Too fine (below 0.1 mm) causes dust and poor flow. Too coarse (above 3 mm) dissolves slowly. To measure PSD, use a set of sieves: 0.1 mm, 0.5 mm, 1 mm, 2 mm, and 3 mm. Stack them with the coarsest on top. Put 100 g of powder on the top sieve and shake for 5 minutes by hand or with a sieve shaker. Weigh the powder on each sieve. Calculate percentages. A good spray-dried powder has: 10â20% below 0.1 mm, 40â60% between 0.1 and 0.5 mm, 20â30% between 0.5 and 1 mm, and less than 5% above 2 mm. If you have too many fines, increase binder in agglomeration or reduce atomizer pressure in spray drying. If too many coarse particles, increase atomizer pressure or reduce binder. For fluid bed granulation, adjust spray rate and air velocity. In Africa, you can buy a set of sieves from a laboratory supplier for about $200. Or make your own from mosquito netting and metal rings. Always take a sample from the middle of the batch, not the top or bottom. Record results in a notebook. If PSD is off, adjust your process and re-test. For consistent product, blend different batches to meet the target. Store powders in a dry placeâmoisture makes particles stick together and changes PSD. Use a moisture meter (cost $50â$100) to check. Aim for less than 3% moisture. For hand-dishwashing powders, a slightly coarser PSD (0.5â2 mm) is preferred because it feels less dusty. For machine powders, finer is better for quick dissolution.

lessons.title: Dust control and explosion prevention
lessons.body: Detergent dust is not just a nuisanceâit can explode. Fine organic and inorganic powders (like sodium lauryl sulphate or sodium carbonate) can form explosive clouds if ignited. In Africa, many small plants ignore this and risk lives. To prevent explosions: first, control dust at the source. Enclose conveyors, mixers, and sieving machines. Use local exhaust ventilation (LEV) with a fan pulling air away from the operator. A simple LEV hood over a sieving station costs $300â$500. Second, ground all metal equipment. Static electricity can spark. Use copper wire to bond bins, pipes, and mixers to a ground rod. Third, use explosion-proof motors and switches in dusty areas. If not available, put motors outside the dust zone and use belt drives. Fourth, keep the workplace clean. Never let dust accumulate on floors or beamsâsweep or vacuum daily. Do not use compressed air to blow dust; it creates a cloud. Use a vacuum with a HEPA filter. Fifth, install a pressure relief vent on any enclosed dust collector. A burst panel (cost $200) directs explosion pressure outdoors. Sixth, train workers to wear N95 masks and goggles. Dust irritates eyes and lungs; long-term exposure causes breathing problems. In humid climates, dust is less likely to become airborne, but still dangerous. Test your dust: take a small sample, try to ignite it with a match in a safe outdoor area. If it burns quickly, it is explosive. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder type) near every process. Never smoke or use open flames. For small-scale production, the biggest risk is from sieving and bag filling. Do those tasks in a separate room with good ventilation. If you cannot afford explosion-proof equipment, do granulation (which reduces dust) instead of selling fine powders.

lessons.title: Quality parameters for powders
lessons.body: To sell detergent powder in Africa, you must meet basic quality standards. Key parameters: moisture content, bulk density, flowability, solubility, pH, and active matter. Moisture: should be below 3% for stable storage. Use a moisture meter or dry a 10 g sample in an oven at 105Â°C for 2 hours; weight loss is moisture. Bulk density: free-flowing powder should be 0.5â0.9 g/mL. Measure by pouring 100 g into a 250 mL graduated cylinder and tapping 20 times. Read volume; density = weight/volume. If density is too low, powder is fluffy and bags will be large. Too high, it dissolves slowly. Flowability: test by pouring powder through a funnel with a 10 mm opening. It should flow freely without shaking. If it sticks, add 1â2% anti-caking agent (sodium aluminosilicate or magnesium stearate). Solubility: stir 5 g in 100 mL water at 30Â°C for 1 minute. It should dissolve completely with no lumps. If not, increase the amount of sodium carbonate or reduce particle size. pH: make a 1% solution and measure with a pH meter or litmus paper. For hand dishwash, pH 7â9 is safe. For machine dishwash, pH 10â12 is normal. Active matter: this is the actual detergent (e.g., linear alkylbenzene sulphonate). For hand wash, 15â25% active matter. For machine, 20â30%. Test by titration with a standard solutionâor send a sample to a local university lab for $20. Also check appearance: uniform colour, no lumps, no foreign matter. Packaging: use laminated bags (PET/PE) to keep out moisture. Store on pallets, not on the floor. In Africa, buyers often check foam height: shake 1 g in 100 mL waterâfoam should last at least 2 minutes. If not, adjust the surfactant. Keep a batch record for every production run. If a batch fails, do not sell itârework it into the next batch. Consistency builds trust and repeat customers.

quiz.q: What is the typical inlet air temperature for a spray dryer used in detergent production?
quiz.explanation: Spray dryers need high inlet temperatures (200â300Â°C) to evaporate water quickly from droplets.

quiz.q: In spray drying, what happens if the outlet air temperature drops below 80Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Low outlet temperature means insufficient drying, leaving powder sticky and prone to caking.

quiz.q: Which part of a spray dryer is most critical for consistent particle size?
quiz.explanation: The atomizer breaks slurry into droplets; worn or wrong settings cause lumps or fines.

quiz.q: For a spinning disc atomizer, what speed range is typical?
quiz.explanation: Spinning disc atomizers operate at high speeds (10,000â20,000 rpm) to create fine droplets.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cyclone in a spray drying system?
options: B) Separate fine dust from exhaust air
quiz.explanation: Cyclones use centrifugal force to separate dried powder particles from the air stream.

quiz.q: In agglomeration, what is a typical binder used for detergent powders?
quiz.explanation: Sodium silicate solution is a common binder that helps particles stick together without harming detergent performance.

quiz.q: What is the recommended particle size for detergent granules?
quiz.explanation: Granules of 0.5â2 mm flow well, dissolve quickly, and produce less dust.

quiz.q: In a pan granulator, what is the typical disc angle?
quiz.explanation: A 45â50 degree angle allows granules to roll and grow uniformly before discharging.

quiz.q: After granulation, what moisture content should granules have before packing?
quiz.explanation: Moisture below 5% prevents caking and microbial growth during storage.

quiz.q: What is a common anti-caking agent for detergent powders?
quiz.explanation: Sodium aluminosilicate absorbs moisture and keeps particles free-flowing.

quiz.q: In a fluid bed dryer, what air velocity is typical for 1â2 mm granules?
quiz.explanation: 1.5â2.5 m/s lifts granules without blowing them out of the bed.

quiz.q: What happens if the bed temperature in a fluid bed granulator drops below 40Â°C?
options: A) Particles become sticky and defluidize
quiz.explanation: Low temperature prevents proper drying, causing particles to stick together and stop fluidizing.

quiz.q: Which coating material is commonly used to protect detergent powder from moisture?
quiz.explanation: PEG 4000 forms a moisture barrier and is safe for detergents.

quiz.q: Why should you ground all metal equipment in a powder plant?
options: A) To prevent static electricity sparks
quiz.explanation: Static sparks can ignite dust clouds, causing explosions; grounding safely discharges static.

quiz.q: What is a safe method to clean up detergent dust?
quiz.explanation: A HEPA vacuum captures fine dust without creating a dangerous airborne cloud.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for most detergent powders?
quiz.explanation: Moisture below 3% ensures free flow and long shelf life.

quiz.q: How do you measure bulk density of a powder?
options: A) Weigh 100 g, pour into 250 mL cylinder, tap 20 times, read volume
quiz.explanation: Bulk density is mass per unit volume after tapping; this method is simple and standard.

quiz.q: What does a flowability test using a funnel with a 10 mm opening indicate?
quiz.explanation: If powder flows freely through the funnel without shaking, it has good flowability.

quiz.q: For hand dishwashing powder, what pH range is considered safe?
quiz.explanation: pH 7â9 is mild on skin yet effective for hand dishwashing.

quiz.q: What is the typical active matter content for machine dishwashing powder?
quiz.explanation: Machine dishwash powders need higher active matter (20â30%) to remove tough grease.

quiz.q: Why is it important to take a PSD sample from the middle of a batch?
options: B) To get a representative sample
C) Because top is always dry
quiz.explanation: The middle of a batch is most representative; top and bottom may segregate by size.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for explosive dust?
options: B) Try to ignite a small sample outdoors
quiz.explanation: If a small sample burns quickly when ignited in a safe area, it is explosive.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a burst panel on a dust collector?
options: A) To release pressure from an explosion
quiz.explanation: A burst panel opens to vent explosion pressure outdoors, protecting equipment and workers.

quiz.q: Which sieve size would you use to check for particles larger than 2 mm?
quiz.explanation: A 2 mm sieve retains particles larger than 2 mm, allowing you to weigh oversize.

quiz.q: In spray drying, what does a slurry solids content of 60â70% mean?
quiz.explanation: Solids content refers to the percentage of dry detergent materials in the slurry.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of nozzle clogging in spray drying?
quiz.explanation: Undissolved solids or foreign matter can block the small nozzle opening.

quiz.q: For fluid bed granulation, what is the effect of increasing spray rate?
quiz.explanation: More binder leads to more particle collisions and growth, forming larger granules.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to reduce dust during sieving?
options: B) Enclose the sieve and use local exhaust ventilation
quiz.explanation: Enclosing the sieve and pulling air away captures dust before it escapes.

quiz.q: Which packaging material is best for keeping detergent powder dry in humid African climates?
quiz.explanation: Laminated bags provide a moisture barrier, preventing caking and loss of quality.

quiz.q: What should you do if a batch of detergent powder fails quality tests?
options: B) Rework it into the next batch
quiz.explanation: Reworking failed batches saves material and maintains product consistency without selling poor quality.
